hallmark: the needle abdomen, the pale antehumeral stripes and the blue tail-light on the eighth segment

reference.title: British Dragonflies (Odonata), plate XXIV, lower pair

doc: *Ischnura elegans*, dorsal — the blue-tailed damselfly, male.
The second plate from Lucas's *British Dragonflies* (1900), after the
southern hawker, and chosen for the contrast: the two animals are the same
order and nothing else. `references/ischnura-elegans.jpg` is plate XXIV,
where the damselfly is the lower pair and the upper pair is *Ischnura
pumilio*; the right-hand lower figure is the one traced.
## What the drawing has to get right
The **build**. A damselfly is a hawker with everything taken away: an
abdomen thirty-eight units across in a body a thousand long, against the
hawker's seventy-eight, and wings that are narrow lenses on a stalk rather
than the hawker's broad triangles. `bodyShape` says `slender` for both,
which is as much as a closed union can say; the plates say the rest, and
side by side on the contact sheet they say it immediately.
On the animals the ratio is nearer three to one than two — a hawker's
abdomen is a tenth of its length and a damselfly's a twenty-fifth. The
hawker's plate draws its own a little narrow, which is a note for whoever
redraws it rather than something to fix here by drawing this one wrong.
Then the **stripes**, which are what the record's `markings` means here: two
pale antehumeral stripes down the thorax, running head to tail, the
character a reader is asked about. Drawn as capsules clipped to the thorax,
so they cannot slide off it.
Then the **tail-light**. Segment eight is bright blue and segments seven and
nine are not, which is the whole of the English name and the quickest way to
tell this animal from the several other blue damselflies. Drawn as bare
paper on the midline, clipped to the abdomen, at the eighth of the ten
segments the ring lines mark out.
## Lucas draws one side at a time
The same problem the hawker had, and the same answer. Lucas spreads each
figure's wings to one side and its legs to the other so the two do not
overlap on the page; the animal has both on both sides, so the wings are
measured off one side, the legs off the other, and each is authored on the
right half for the renderer to reflect.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front of the head, y = 1000 at the tip of the abdomen. The
thorax is 76 to 258 — a fifth of the animal — and everything after it is
abdomen. The four wings spring from the thorax and reach past x = 610; the legs are short and held forward, and only the fore tarsi pass above y = 0.

note: The legs first, so they pass under the wings and the body.
Short, fine and held forward: a damselfly catches small flies in a basket
made of its own legs, which is why all six point ahead of the thorax
rather than out from it. The spines Lucas draws on each tibia are left
out — at eighty pixels they are a furred outline.
The hind wing. Narrow, stalked at the base and rounded at the tip — a
lens rather than the hawker’s triangle, and the shape that separates the
damselflies from the dragonflies at a glance.
`membrane`, so what is behind it shows through. Four of these overlap each
other and the abdomen, and the point of a damselfly’s wing is that it is
a window.
The venation, as four strokes laid from just inside the leading edge to
just inside the trailing one.
Five, closer together, was the first pass, and at plate size they merged
into one dark line down the middle of the wing — which is worse than no
venation at all, because a wing with a spine through it is not a wing.
Lucas draws several hundred cells; four is what survives at eighty pixels.
The pterostigma: the one opaque cell near the leading edge, three
quarters of the way out. Small, and drawn because it is the only mark on
an otherwise clear wing.
The fore wing, and where it is attached matters as much as its shape.
Both wings spring from the thorax — 76 to 258 in plate space — and hold
out to the side, angled a little towards the head. The first pass had
them leaving the animal at y = 470, which is a third of the way down the
abdomen, and it read as a dragonfly with its wings on backwards. Lucas
draws all four bases inside the length of the synthorax and that is where
they are now.
The abdomen: ten segments and almost nothing across them. Thirty units
wide against the hawker's hundred and sixty, and the slight swelling
towards the tip is the eighth and ninth segments, which is where the blue
is.
The segment rings, as eight strokes each crossing the axis.
This is the case the fan validator allows on the midline: both guides are
centred on x = 0, so every stroke straddles it and `mirror: false` is
true of each one. Authored on the right half instead, they would be eight
half-rings sitting off the axis and the validator would say so.
The tail-light. Segment eight, and only segment eight: bare paper on the
axis, clipped to the abdomen so it cannot reach past the animal's own
edge.
The claspers at the tip of the abdomen, which is how a male damselfly
holds a female behind the head. Small, and the reason this plate commits
to a sex.
The synthorax: the box the four wings and the six legs all hang off, and
a fifth of the animal's length.
The antehumeral stripes, which is what `markings: 'stripes'` means on
this record: two pale lines running head to tail down the thorax, with
the darker humeral stripe outside each. Clipped to the thorax, so a
stripe cannot end up beside the animal.
The head. Transverse and mostly eye — the central part is narrow and the
two compound eyes are the whole of the width, which is why the head
outline here is narrower than the animal is across.
A compound eye. Set well apart, which is the character that separates a
damselfly's head from a hawker's — a hawker's eyes meet on top of its
head and these do not come close.
The antenna: two short bristles, which is all an Odonata has and the
reason `REQUIRED_PARTS` does not ask this order for them. Drawn anyway,
because the record says `setaceous` and this is the drawing of that word.
